snippet.title: COMPASSION FATIGUE EXPLAINED-SIGNS, SYMPTOMS AND SOLUTIONS FOR PARENT CARE
snippet.description:
Are you an adult child caring for an aging parent? If so, you’re probably familiar with the emotional highs and lows that come with this journey. In this video, we’ll talk about compassion fatigue—a common experience for family caregivers—and explore how it affects those of us caring for elderly parents or loved ones. We’ll dive into the signs and symptoms of compassion fatigue, how it shows up in our daily lives, and what you can do to support your own mental health while still being there for your parent.

What You’ll Learn:
What is Compassion Fatigue? We’ll define compassion fatigue and explain why it’s common in caregiving for aging parents.
Signs and Symptoms – Recognize when you’re feeling drained, emotionally exhausted, or detached from your loved ones, which may be signs of caregiver burnout.
Self-Care Tips for Caregivers – Learn practical self-care strategies and routines to help you recharge and prevent compassion fatigue from taking over.
Preventing Caregiver Burnout – We’ll discuss ways to set boundaries, manage caregiving stress, and protect your mental health as a family caregiver.
How to Manage Compassion Fatigue – Discover how mindfulness, boundary-setting, and mental health support can make a real difference.
This video is packed with self-care tips for caregivers that are simple, effective, and designed to help you maintain compassion for your parent without sacrificing your own well-being. Whether you’re providing support daily, helping from a distance, or balancing elder care with work, these tools and insights will help you manage the pressures of caregiving more effectively.

Keywords:
Compassion fatigue in caregiving, caring for aging parents without burnout, signs of compassion fatigue, self-care tips for caregivers, supporting elderly parents without stress, preventing caregiver burnout, managing compassion fatigue, caregiver mental health, caregiver support for compassion fatigue

Who Is This Video For?
If you’re feeling overwhelmed by caregiving or noticing symptoms like irritability, emotional exhaustion, or physical fatigue, this video is for you. Compassion fatigue is a natural response, but with the right support and self-care strategies, you can find relief and continue to care for your loved one from a place of compassion.

snippet.title: Overcoming Caregiver Burnout & Guilt: How Real Families Find Peace in Elder Care
snippet.description:
Are you struggling with caregiver guilt or feeling burnt out taking care of an aging parent at home? In this episode of the Kriti Elder Care Podcast, we sit down with Business Coach Parul, who shares her personal experience after bringing her mother to transition care following a severe chest infection and hospital stay.

Parul talks candidly about the realities of managing oxygen support, balancing a full-time career with caregiving, and overcoming the cultural guilt that many adult children face in India. 

We also explore real family stories—including a relative in the US facing severe caregiver burnout, and a 60+ aunt (Chachi) who stayed as an attendant, joined in on daily Tambola games, tried physiotherapy, and loved the lively social community!

• Managing oxygen care & medical recovery post-hospitalization
• Why stopping your career out of guilt disrupts the whole family system

snippet.title: 82: Caring for Aging Parents from a Distance: Preventing Caregiver Burnout with Janice Goldmintz
snippet.description:
Navigating the care of our aging parents is one of the most profound, yet least talked about, transitions we face as adults. This is really common—we rarely sit down to discuss end-of-life wishes or logistics until a sudden medical crisis throws us into an emotional whirlwind. When you are managing this transition from a distance—whether due to life circumstances or the unique demands of military deployment and relocation—the weight can easily ripple into your marriage, leading to invisible strain and emotional disconnection.  

In this episode, I sit down with gerontologist Janice Goldmintz to explore how couples can navigate these heavy role reversals, manage complex family dynamics, and protect their relationship bond while honoring their parents' autonomy.  What this really means is that you don’t have to carry this heavy weight alone. You’ll walk away with small, practical tools to stay on the same team with your partner, lean on external resources safely, and build your own emotional resilience toolkit so you can thrive, not just survive.

💛 Free Relationship Pattern Assessment
Many couples spend months trying harder, communicating more, or reading another relationship book, only to find themselves having the same argument again.

The issue may not be what you're arguing about—it may be the pattern underneath it.
Take the free Relationship Pattern Assessment and discover what may be keeping you stuck.

RESOURCES:
Want more details from this episode? Check out the full show notes here:
https://www.communicateandconnect.com/podcasts/episode82/


ABOUT OUR GUEST:
Janice Goldmintz is an educator, facilitator, and advocate for adult children navigating the emotional and practical challenges of caring for aging parents. Drawing from both personal experience and academic training, Janice brings a rare depth of compassion and clarity to a process that often feels overwhelming and isolating.

With a Master’s degree in Gerontology and firsthand experience supporting both of her parents through Alzheimer’s disease, Janice understands the shifting terrain of caregiving—from anticipatory grief and family dynamics to complex decision-making around care and quality of life. She helps adult children make sense of the maze of systems, agencies, and conversations involved in elder care, while also tending to their own wellbeing.

Janice is also a certified trainer with Jack Canfield (Chicken Soup for the Soul), integrating mindset and goal-setting tools to help caregivers preserve balance, resilience, and perspective during difficult seasons. Through presentations, family facilitation, and education, her mission is to help older adults live full, dignified lives—and to ensure their children feel supported, informed, and not alone.

Learn more and connect with Janice at www.talkaboutaging.com.

What happens when an aging parent needs care—but the family relationship is strained, estranged, or shaped by unresolved trauma?

Eldercare expert Amy Friesen joins clinical psychologist Dr. Christopher Barker to examine the complicated realities facing adult children who are expected to become caregivers. Society often assumes that every aging parent has built-in family support, but that expectation rarely accounts for childhood trauma, unsafe relationships, family estrangement, financial limitations, or the caregiver’s own health and responsibilities.

Amy explains why caregiving decisions are rarely as simple as asking, “Will you take care of your parents?” For many adult children, stepping back into the family means confronting old attachment patterns, guilt, pressure, and painful dynamics they worked hard to leave.

The conversation also explores caregiver burnout and the “club sandwich generation”—adults simultaneously caring for children, an aging parent, and a spouse who may also need support. When caregivers continually place themselves last, exhaustion can reduce their ability to manage even basic decisions and logistics.

Amy and Dr. Barker discuss the gaps between public and private care systems, hospital discharge challenges, long-term-care waitlists, dementia planning, senior housing, aging in place, and the risks of waiting until a family is already in crisis.

The clearest takeaway: start planning earlier. A will only addresses what happens after death; families also need to discuss powers of attorney, healthcare wishes, caregiving capacity, housing preferences, finances, safety, and boundaries while everyone can still participate.

In this episode:

The pressure placed on adult children to become caregivers
How estrangement and unresolved trauma affect eldercare
Caregiver guilt, burnout, and loss of personal capacity
Setting boundaries with aging parents
The sandwich and “club sandwich” generations
Why families postpone aging and end-of-life planning
Wills, powers of attorney, and advance-care wishes
Dementia and the importance of early planning
Senior housing, retirement living, and long-term care
Gaps between hospitals and public and private care systems
Planning for solo seniors and aging adults with limited income
Why preparing for your own aging is a gift to those around you

About Amy Friesen

Amy Friesen is an eldercare expert, educator, best-selling author, and speaker with more than 20 years of experience helping seniors and caregivers navigate aging, senior housing, and difficult family decisions. She is the founder of Tea & Toast and Eldercare Planners of Canada. Her trauma-informed work addresses caregiver resilience, boundaries, unresolved family trauma, and generational patterns in caregiving.

Learn more about Amy: https://www.amyfriesen.com/

Dr. Christopher Barker is a New Jersey-licensed clinical psychologist and the host of Holding Space, a show featuring thoughtful conversations about psychology, relationships, mental health, and personal growth.

snippet.title: Family Respite for Caregivers
snippet.description:
Caregiver burnout is one of the most significant, yet frequently overlooked, risks facing family members supporting aging relatives.

When a spouse or adult child transitions into a full-time caregiving role, the physical and emotional strain accumulates quickly. Left unchecked, it routinely leads to serious health complications for the caregiver themselves.

Key warning signs of caregiver exhaustion include:
• Chronic sleep disruption
• Persistent fatigue unalleviated by rest
• Unremitting baseline anxiety

Navigating clinical tasks, household management, and personal care can erode the essential parent-child or spousal relationship. Utilizing short-term respite care is not an admission of failure—it is a proactive strategy to protect the caregiver’s well-being and ensure sustainable, high-quality support for the care recipient over time.

Integrating even a few hours of professional home support each week provides critical relief, mitigates burnout risks, and helps preserve family dynamics.

snippet.title: Adult Child Caregiver Burnout: When Is It Time to Ask for Help?
snippet.description:
Caring for an ageing parent can slowly become a second full-time job.

Between work, family responsibilities, appointments, paperwork, medical decisions, and the emotional weight of watching someone you love lose independence, many adult children find themselves carrying far more than they ever expected.

But what happens when caregiving becomes too much to manage alone?

In this episode of **Nervous System Reset for Caregivers**, Michelle speaks with **Wendy Adlerstein**, a licensed social worker with nearly 30 years of experience in ageing and home care.

Together, they explore the often-unspoken reality of adult child caregiving — the exhaustion, racing thoughts, disrupted sleep, guilt, isolation, and constant feeling of being “on.”

Wendy shares practical insights on recognising when a caregiver needs additional support, planning before a crisis happens, introducing home care while protecting an ageing parent’s dignity, and building a care team that supports both the parent and the person providing care.

### In This Episode, You’ll Discover:

• The quiet signs that caregiving may be becoming overwhelming
• Why caring for an ageing parent can feel so isolating
• When it may be time to consider outside support
• How planning ahead can reduce pressure during a crisis
• How to introduce home care without taking away dignity or independence
• Important questions to ask when choosing a home care provider
• Why predictable support can help protect caregiver capacity
• How families can communicate and share caregiving responsibilities
• A simple grounding exercise before a difficult caregiving conversation

### A Simple Step You Can Take Today

You don't have to solve your entire caregiving journey at once.

Take a moment and write down:

**1. What feels hardest right now?**
**2. What would reduce the pressure by 20%?**
**3. Who could help me take the first step?**

Sometimes, making one pressure point visible is the first step toward creating meaningful support.

snippet.title: Caregiver Burnout: Staying a Son/Daughter While Acting as a Nurse During Long Illness
snippet.description:
Being someone’s son or daughter doesn’t end when you start learning to act like a nurse. In long-term illness, the lines between family roles can blur—care becomes constant, responsibilities multiply, and relationships can quietly shift under the pressure of “just getting through the day.” 💛

In this video, we explore the emotional reality behind caregiver-family dynamics: how you can feel like you’re protecting your family identity while also slowly rewriting what your loved one—and yourself—need from you. We’ll discuss why caregiving can create an invisible power imbalance, how exhaustion changes communication, and what happens when everyone has less room to rest, grieve, or be fully seen.

You’ll come away with practical, compassionate insights for navigating these hard seasons, including:

• Recognizing role strain when you become both family and caregiver
• Understanding how constant care can affect boundaries and connection
• Identifying early signs of breakdown—before resentment, burnout, or withdrawal takes over
• Finding ways to maintain dignity, closeness, and “family identity” even under stress
• Approaches to support yourself and keep the relationship from turning into a task list

If you’re caring for a loved one—whether full-time or in hard stretches—this conversation is for you. You deserve support, clarity, and permission to ask what breaks first when no one can rest, so you can protect what matters most.
